title: Span<T>
sub: A window into memory, no copying
cards/0/body: Span<T> is a "window" into a chunk of memory: a start and a length. The memory can be an array, a string, the stack or a native buffer. A slice span[2..5] copies nothing — it is a new window onto the same bytes.
cards/1/q: What is in arr[1] after middle[0] = 20?
cards/1/options/0: 20 — the Span looks at the same array
cards/1/explain: A Span does not own memory; it just looks at it.
cards/2/task: Parsing the string "12,34,56" creates garbage right now. Pick a way that puts not a single object on the heap.
cards/3/q: Why does Split create 4 objects for the string "12,34,56"?
cards/3/options/0: An array for the parts plus three new strings
cards/3/explain: Strings are immutable, so every part is a new string.
cards/4/body:
You can view a string as a ReadOnlySpan<char>: slices without copies, and int.Parse can read straight from a slice.

A small temporary buffer can live on the stack — no heap at all:
cards/4/code:
Span<byte> buf = stackalloc byte[256];
int written = Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("hello", buf);
cards/5/explain: Substring would create a new string.
cards/7/q: What can a Span look at? Select all.
cards/7/explain: Native memory too. A file has to be read into a buffer first.
cards/8/q: Why bother, if the GC cleans up garbage anyway?
cards/8/options/0: Less garbage means fewer collections and pauses; in hot code the difference is huge
cards/8/options/1: The GC cannot clean up strings
cards/8/explain: The fastest object is the one you never created.
